state.misconception_label: Confuses rest and movement on a distance time graph

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: This graph shows how far Fido the dog is from his home. What might the negative-sloping section represent? ![A graph with time (secs) on the horizontal axis and distance (m) on the vertical axis. The graph starts at the origin, travels in a straight line up and right, travels horizontally, then travels in a straight line down and right back to the x-axis. ](). I got Fido has fallen asleep because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you're watching a movie where the main character is running away from something. The negative-sloping section on the distance-time graph could represent the character moving further away from where they started. This is similar to when Fido is running away from his home. Can you see how the negative slope represents movement away from the starting point?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, I think I get it a bit better now! So, the negative slope means Fido is actually moving away from home instead of just resting? But what about when the line goes flat? Does that mean he's just standing still or something?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you're looking at a speed-time graph of a car. When the line goes flat, it means the car is maintaining a constant speed, not standing still. Just like the car is still moving even when the line is flat, Fido could still be moving even when the distance-time graph is horizontal.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher provides mathematically incorrect explanations (claiming negative slope means moving away and horizontal means moving on a distance-time graph), fails to address the student's actual misconception about rest vs. movement, and the student remains confused by the end, even asking about the horizontal section which the teacher then explains incorrectly.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher attempts to use concrete analogies (movie character, car), they fundamentally misinterpret the graph by claiming negative slope means moving away when it actually means returning home, undermining the experiential approach's effectiveness.
